#2810. The missing Gen-Z reaction that told JJ Redick this Lakers team was special

Long before the Lakers were the best story in the NBA, JJ Redick had an inkling that this team was different.

It clicked for him after the Lakers had a team dinner at Carbone Riviera in Las Vegas in July.

After general manager Rob Pelinka paid the bill, Redick became hyperaware of what had not happened that evening.

"I get up to leave and it struck me," he said. "Nobody had left. Nobody had been on their phone."

But they were indicative of the character of the group. The players wanted to bond. They wanted to be around one another.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic reacts to a charging foul during a game against the Charlotte Hornets, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in Los Angeles. Getty Images

They were in Sin City, surrounded by a million distractions, but they chose to spend their time with one another.

Now a team that was expected to be a mile behind the Thunder and Spurs in the Western Conference has the best record in the league at 13-2. They've won nine games in a row. They've announced themselves as real championship contenders.

The Lakers have surpassed expectations. They're leading the league in offensive rating (123.1) and steals (10.8) and they're third in blocks (6.1).

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick calls out directions against the Portland Trail Blazers in Los Angeles on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Getty Images

Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves constantly tease each other as though they were brothers. Their affinity for one another has spilled onto the court, where they're the top-scoring duo in the league, averaging a combined 63.5 points per game.

Walker Kessler has a contagious positivity. He's also a beast down low and a double-double machine, averaging 14.5 points and 10.9 rebounds per game.

And the Lakers' role players are starring in their roles.

That was never more obvious than in the Lakers' 118-114 overtime win over the Hornets on Tuesday. The Lakers were without Kessler (right lower leg soreness) and Reaves (left heel bruise). Doncic was in foul trouble. The Lakers trailed by as much as 18 points.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic, left, slaps hands with head coach JJ Redick during an NBA game Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, in Los Angeles. AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill

Doncic realized Quentin Grimes had a hot hand. He started waving off Redick's play calls in the fourth quarter, so he could feed his teammate. Grimes went on to finish with a career-high 47 points, becoming the only Laker to score 10 or more 3-pointers in a game other than Kobe Bryant in the Lakers' win.

Things have just come together for the Lakers.

There's a good feeling in the locker room. The guys genuinely like each other. And that's dangerous for the rest of the league.

"I think at the end of the day we have great chemistry, which is in my opinion very important," Doncic said. "But I think this group is very special."

It's interesting because the Lakers weren't supposed to jell this quickly.

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick looks on against the Atlanta Hawks during the fourth quarter at State Farm Arena in Atlanta on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Getty Images

They have nine new players. Doncic has never been known as a vocal leader. This was supposed to be a transition year after LeBron James left in free agency and the Lakers overhauled their roster around the Slovenian superstar.

But something happened over the summer that changed things.

A seed was planted in Vegas. And it flourished after Doncic flew his teammates to Slovenia to host a mini camp, something he had never done before in his career.

They laughed. They sightsaw. They bonded with each other and grew a much deeper understanding of their biggest star.

Redick believes what's happening right now is a magical coalescence of opportunity meeting the right personnel.

It has resulted in a locker room with good vibes. A team that's soaring. And a coach who is deeply grateful that his gut feeling was correct.

He first saw it months ago, long before they ever stepped foot on the court.

"I don't know what this is going to look like after 82 games," Redick said. "I don't know what it's going to look like after 50. But I do know that there's something with this group. Every special group doesn't mean you win a championship.

#2809. Fed’s Waller says central bank may need to ‘shock people’ with half-point rate hike

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation, saying the central bank needs to "shock people" as prices continue to rise more than he expected.

In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half percentage point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.

He said the central bank needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more.

"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a "Squawk Box" interview. "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions."

"You might need to, like, shock people," he said.

Futures prices are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the FOMC's December meeting. They also are anticipating another move in January, followed by at least one additional increase before the end of 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge.

Waller said the Fed wouldn't necessarily have to approve a half-point hike in December if it raised rates by a quarter point and signaled another move coming in January. However, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on grounds that it ties policymakers' hands.

"If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets, you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 [basis points] in December to put it in place and get it done," he said.

Recent statements from other central bankers indicate a range of opinions, though most agree that more policy tightening is needed to bring down inflation.

In a speech Tuesday, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027. Some Fed officials, including regional Presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Lorie Logan of Dallas, have endorsed more gradual tightening.

However, continued inflation above the Fed's 2% target might push officials into a more aggressive stance.

The FOMC approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years in September, and then held rates steady at its October meeting. While inflation has continued to run hot since then, other Fed officials seem less eager to drop the policy hammer as heavily as Waller.

"I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday in a conversation with Axios. "I think what we've been doing over the last past few months is ... working well. We're collecting the data, analyzing it, having the debate and making a decision."

The Fed in 2025 approved three rate cuts amid worries over the labor market and the belief that inflation would continue to moderate toward the central bank's 2% goal.

However, inflation reignited earlier this year after the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran in late February. Energy prices spiked while tariff impacts lingered, keeping most inflation readings above 3%.

"First of all, you've got to take back the three insurance cuts we put in last year," Waller said. "If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn't bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn't going to bring it down. So we may have to go above ... three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down."

The FOMC later Wednesday will release minutes from the October meeting.

#2808. Inside India newsletter: Foreign flows helped the market recover. Now it faces the inflation test

Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

As global portfolio managers look to diversify into non-artificial intelligence trades, India, with its strong economic growth and improved corporate earnings, is emerging as a top pick. But the country's inflation, which has been rising for 12 straight months, could impede inflows.

Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.

Foreign investors are returning to Indian equities in record numbers, but the country's accelerating inflation, which last month breached the central bank's comfort level for the first time in two years, could spoil the party.

India's retail inflation rose to 6.09% ​in October, crossing the Reserve Bank of India's 6% upper limit, driven by surging food and transport costs.

Experts told CNBC that businesses have already started passing on increased costs to consumers, with signs of slowing demand visible in the rural economy and expected to hurt urban consumption by early next year.

"Rising inflation will squeeze household real incomes, while higher interest rates will weigh on investment and consumption, potentially putting pressure on corporate earnings," Alexandra Hermann Prasad, lead economist at Oxford Economics, told CNBC.

That could "temper foreign investor enthusiasm in the near term, even if India's structural growth prospects remain attractive," she added.

High-frequency indicators like car sales and credit card transactions softened in September while air passenger traffic declined for the fourth month in a row, Indian brokerage HDFC Securities said in a report on Tuesday.

As per data from the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, released on Nov. 6, car sales fell 14.2% year on year in October. The industry body said that its "pressing concern is inventory" with dealers, which was elevated at 45 days in September and October, as against the usual range of 30 days. The inflation print "is not good," Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at India's IDFC First Bank, told CNBC, adding that inflation pressures led by supply-side shocks are spreading, and if that persists, it will affect corporate margins and household consumption.

She expects the RBI to raise benchmark rates by 25 basis points each over the next three monetary policies, taking the terminal interest rate to 6.25% by April next year.

The tightening of monetary policy is also likely to slow the recovery of the private investment cycle, denting India's economic outlook, experts said.

So far in November, foreign investors have pumped in more than $10 billion net in Indian equities. If that sustains, it will be the highest ever foreign capital inflow in a single month.

This would be a sharp contrast to earlier this year in March when foreign investors pulled a record $12 billion from India on worries that the energy shock from the Iran war could squeeze the economy and slow growth.

India's growth story, however, has remained intact so far, with corporate earnings showing a sharp improvement over the last two quarters. That resilience, alongside a rotation from AI names, has drawn investors back to India, as they look to diversify into non-artificial intelligence trades.

The fall in oil prices and the easing of tensions between Iran and the U.S. after the midterm poll results have also worked in India's favor, though experts warn that it is still too early to call November's rebound of foreign capital "a structural reversal."

"November's return of capital inflows primarily reflects lower oil prices, changing global risk sentiment following the US midterm elections, and growing concerns about the sustainability of the AI cycle, rather than a clear structural shift towards Indian assets," Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific Economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, told CNBC.

That makes rising inflation a big worry for sustained inflows. Higher inflation could further weaken household demand, prompt monetary tightening, and slow earnings growth, making the return on Indian assets "less attractive," Luchnikava-Schorsch said.

India relies on imports to meet 85% of its crude needs and around 50% of its supplies transited through the Strait of Hormuz before the Iran war. Energy supply disruptions due to the Iran war have led to a sharp rise in inflation across several major economies in the world, including India.

"What matters more for attracting stable, long-term capital, and for weathering short-term swings in flows, is whether India can sustain the high growth path it is on," Madhavi Bokil, executive director, credit strategy & standards at Moody's Ratings, told CNBC, adding that higher inflation is a risk to that path.

India's inflation crosses 6% in October after rising for 12 straight monthsIndia's retail inflation rose to 6.09% ​in October, crossing the Reserve Bank of India's 6% limit for the first time under the new series, owing to surging food prices. Inflation has been on the rise for 12 straight months in the South Asian country.

#2806. Nuggets Overcome 17-Point Deficit To Stun Celtics; 5 Key Takeaways

The Denver Nuggets pulled off an impressive comeback to stun the Boston Celtics 105-101, overcoming a 17-point deficit to steal a road victory. Boston controlled much of the game and led for 79% of the contest, but Denver found another gear when it mattered most, turning a difficult night into a statement win.

Nikola Jokic led the Nuggets with 24 points, eight rebounds, and nine assists, while Jamal Murray added 21 points and seven rebounds. DeMar DeRozan also provided a major boost off the bench with 18 points, giving Denver the scoring punch it needed to complete the comeback.

Boston had several strong individual performances. Jayson Tatum finished with 24 points and eight rebounds, Neemias Queta recorded 17 points and 10 rebounds, and Payton Pritchard contributed 15 points. However, the Celtics struggled to capitalize on their early advantage, and Denver's ability to get to the free-throw line proved decisive.

Here are five key takeaways from Denver's comeback victory.

When the Nuggets needed their stars to deliver, Jokic and Murray answered.

Jokic finished with 24 points, eight rebounds, and nine assists on 9-17 shooting. He came close to another triple-double while providing Denver with the offensive organization and decision-making that make him so difficult to defend.

Murray added 21 points, seven rebounds, and four steals in 38 minutes. His defensive activity was particularly impressive, and his ability to contribute across multiple areas helped Denver stay competitive as the game developed.

Together, the two stars accounted for 45 points, 15 rebounds, and 11 assists. That production gave Denver a dependable foundation even when the team was struggling to find consistent offense elsewhere.

The Nuggets did not need one player to score 40 points to complete this comeback. They needed their two best players to control the game, make the right decisions, and keep the offense functioning. Jokic and Murray did exactly that.

DeRozan was arguably Denver's most important supporting player in this victory. The veteran finished with 18 points on 5-11 shooting, adding seven assists and eight free-throw attempts.

His ability to create offense gave the Nuggets another option beyond Jokic and Murray. While Denver's starting lineup provided the foundation, DeRozan's contribution off the bench helped keep the scoring pressure on Boston.

He also showed why having an experienced shot creator can be valuable during a comeback. DeRozan can generate opportunities without needing the offense to revolve entirely around him, and his playmaking helped Denver maintain offensive balance.

The Nuggets received only limited scoring from several other reserves, making DeRozan's 18 points even more significant. In a four-point victory, that kind of bench production can make all the difference.

The Celtics appeared to be in control for much of the night, but their shooting struggles ultimately caught up with them.

Boston shot just 40-98 from the field, finishing at 40.8%. The Celtics also went 11-44 from three-point range, converting only 25.0% of their attempts.

Tatum led the team with 24 points, while Queta added 17 points and 10 rebounds. Pritchard contributed 15 points, and Derrick White recorded 12 points and eight assists. However, Boston did not receive enough consistent offensive production to maintain its advantage.

Paul George struggled to find his rhythm, finishing with 10 points on 3-12 shooting, including 1-7 from beyond the arc. His limited scoring was another challenge for a Celtics team that needed more reliable production as Denver mounted its comeback.

Boston actually made more three-pointers than Denver, 11-7, but the overall shooting efficiency was poor. The Celtics had plenty of opportunities to put the game away and failed to convert enough of them.

One of the biggest statistical differences was Denver's ability to get to the free-throw line.

The Nuggets attempted 29 free throws and converted 24, while Boston attempted just 12 and made 10. That gave Denver a massive 14-point advantage in made free throws.

The difference was especially important because neither team shot particularly well from three-point range. Denver made only seven of 31 attempts, while Boston converted 11 of 44.

Rather than depending on perimeter shooting, the Nuggets found another way to generate offense by attacking and drawing fouls. DeRozan led that effort with eight free-throw attempts, while Murray added five and Jokic contributed three.

Boston's 30 personal fouls compared to Denver's 13 also tells an important part of the story. The Celtics struggled to defend without sending the Nuggets to the line, allowing Denver to keep adding points even when its field-goal offense was inconsistent.

The Celtics recorded 22 assists compared to Denver's 19, grabbed 18 offensive rebounds compared to 14, and outscored the Nuggets 48-34 in the paint. Boston also forced Denver into 18 turnovers, two more than its own total.

However, the Nuggets made up for those disadvantages through better shooting efficiency, transition opportunities, and free-throw production. Denver shot 43.5% from the field compared to Boston's 40.8% and finished with an 18-14 advantage in fast-break points.

Murray's four steals also helped Denver generate defensive stops, while the team collectively found enough ways to disrupt Boston's offensive rhythm.

The most impressive part was Denver's ability to stay composed despite trailing by 17 points. Boston controlled the scoreboard for most of the game, but the Nuggets kept competing until the momentum finally shifted.

#2805. Vance scraps schedule to address tech outages as Trump admin insists incidents aren't linked

Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday abruptly canceled his scheduled appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit to instead attend meetings on a recent wave of high-profile technology outages.

The cancellation was announced shortly after a senior Trump administration official insisted that the outages, which have affected a wide range of industries and have been felt across the country and around the world, are not the result of a cyberattack or any form of coordinated action.

"We have a great deal of confidence in our assessment that these incidents are the result of upgrades of the systems, systems being patched, hardware being applied" or other "disparate" events, the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the government's intelligence assessments.

The official briefed news outlets by phone in the wake of numerous major disruptions at large corporations and federal agencies in recent days, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a protracted Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network.

Other incidents include software issues at JPMorgan Chase, an outage at United Airlines that caused some flight delays and product issues at Apple.

On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC that the outages are not a cyberattack and "not a coordinated effort by a nation-state."

He gave a similar assurance on Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee.

"We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton said. "We also have no indication that they're result of a state-sponsored malign actor."

But the sheer volume of incidents in the past week alone has raised alarm bells among consumers and tech experts alike, with some wondering if rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models are to blame.

The senior Trump administration official, asked on Wednesday's call to what degree AI was involved in the outages, said it is "challenging to answer that question across all of these incidents that have been reported."

Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told CNBC on Wednesday morning he wants "better coordination" on AI safety.

"I understand why people are freaked out," Warner said. "The one way we could lose this AI race and [see] all of these companies' valuations plummet dramatically is if we have an AI tool run amok, or an AI-sponsored cyberattack that creates harm."

His comments came hours before before Anthropic is scheduled to price its initial public offering for the first major AI industry IPO.

Warner advocated for a "pre-testing regime" for new AI models that establishes guardrails and helps ensure a "culture of safety built in" to the industry."

He said the U.S. is "lucky" that it has so far avoided a major AI-generated cyberattack or a crisis with a rogue agent that goes beyond incidents like the Hugging Face breach earlier this year.

— CNBC's Samantha Subin contributed to this report.

#2804. Phillies Making “Serious” Push for Teruaki Sato

The Philadelphia Phillies have had a slow start to the offseason, at least in terms of player acquisition. They have not made any substantial moves this offseason, and their roster still has plenty of holes.

The Phillies are trying to make the most of their rapidly closing World Series window, and signing another impact bat would help. One player the Phillies have shown plenty of interest in is Japanese third baseman Teruaki Sato. He is the best player available on the international market, and many expect him to be an impact bat in MLB.

The Phillies are expected to let Alec Bohm walk in free agency, opening a spot at third base. Sato is expected to be their main target to fill the role. According to Patrick Gordon, the Phillies are making a "serious" push for Sato. A source in the NPB also indicated that the Phillies have had more contact with Sato than any other club.

In the past, the Phillies have not been active in signing Japanese players. However, seeing some of the players who have come over in recent years (Ohtani, Yamamoto, Murakami), the Phillies would be foolish not to dip their toe in that water.

Sato could be an impact bat in the middle of the Phillies lineup. Last season in the Japan Central League, Sato hit .306 with 39 home runs and 106 RBIs. Those numbers were good enough for the Triple Crown. Interestingly enough, the last player to win the NPB Triple Crown was Murakami, who signed with the Chicago White Sox last offseason.

The 27-year-old Sato is entering the prime of his career, and his skills should translate to MLB. The only issue with his offensive profile is his strikeout rate. Sato struck out 164 times in 614 plate appearances, a 26.7% strikeout rate. His swing-and-miss issue will only get attacked more against better MLB pitchers. However, the Phillies just hired Peter Fatse, and helping Sato with his approach could be one of his first tasks.

Sato not only plays third base, but he also has corner outfield experience. That gives the Phillies flexibility to move him around if they can acquire other impact players. The transition to MLB won't be easy for Sato, but based on how his Japanese counterparts have done in the past, it is a risk the Phillies should take.

#2801. One of the world's most contested seas is proving too much for Asia's leaders to resolve

One of the world's most contested bodies of water continues to cause problems for Asia's leaders.

A substantive Code of Conduct in the South China Sea does not seem to be feasible despite ASEAN nations expressing optimism that the negotiations could finally conclude after more than two decades, experts told CNBC.

The ASEAN summit in the Philippines failed to resolve it, despite Manila saying it intended to conclude the Code this year.

The crux of the issue is that China claims virtually all of the South China Sea as its own territory, despite international rulings saying it's not the case and historical claims from many other countries.

China's "nine-dash line" claim was ruled as invalid by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, although Beijing has refused to recognize that ruling.

Over decades, China has been building shoals into structures that strengthen its territorial assertions, and has become increasingly aggressive in policing the territory against nations such as the Philippines, that claim traditional rights over the maritime areas.

The Code of Conduct for the South China Sea aims to address areas where multiple ASEAN nations and China have disputes and competing claims.

Manila has reported that it had completed 80% of the negotiating text, with negotiations to continue under next ASEAN chair Singapore. But, experts are skeptical that a "substantive and effective" agreement can be realized, at least in the short term.

"It's an annual ritual. The ASEAN Chair commits to completing the Code of Conduct in January, but by November is reporting that — although great progress has been made — they didn't quite get there this year. Rinse, repeat," Ray Powell, executive director at gray-zone activities tracker SeaLight Foundation told CNBC.He described the 80% number as "a meaningless statistic," given that the issue at hand was complex and contentious.

ASEAN secretary general Kao Kim Hourn still sees potential for resolution. "I don't think it's a failure at all," he told CNBC's JP Ong. "There's still a lot of commitment and a lot of leadership on both sides to move ahead and get it done."

But Collin Koh, senior fellow at the Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies in Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told CNBC that even if 80% of the text has been set, the 20% remaining contain the most persistent problems, including geographical scope, competing interests among ASEAN member states, and enforcement.

Koh said the original aim was ASEAN to negotiate with China "one-to-one," but, it has never been the case.

"It has always been 10 against one. Now you add Timor Leste. Now 11 against one. So, because of that, there is never any unified ASEAN position that they will bring to the table with with China," he pointed out.

Disputes in the South China Sea stretch at least as far back as the 1970s, with various countries such as Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam claiming various zones and islands in the critical maritime region, which houses rich natural resources and fishing areas.

Back in 2015, Singapore has positioned itself as a "neutral broker" in ASEAN-China dialogue, with then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong saying that Singapore will deal "fairly and openly with all parties" in order to "preserve peace and stability in the region."

But while the city-state may be able to broker some compromises, the disagreements that have held up the code for almost a quarter of a century will persist, according to Lynn Kuok, Lee Kuan Yew Chair of Southeast Asia Studies at the Brookings Institution.

"Beijing, moreover, has little incentive to accept meaningful restraints while it continues to consolidate its position in the South China Sea," Kuok added.

Her view was echoed by Joshua Kurlantzick, senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, who said that a code of conduct is unlikely to happen soon, if ever. "China at its heart doesn't really want a code of conduct, and it continues to push more assertively into the South China Sea." He pointed out Beijing's actions against the Philippines in the region, including around the disputed Scarborough Shoal.

Chinese coast guard vessels have most recently been accused of ramming Filipino fishing vessels near the Spratly islands in September, and have used lasers and water cannons against Filipino ships in the past.

Kurlantzick also said that there are multiple countries within ASEAN that are close to China that are willing to hold up any agreement on the Code, adding that the move toward China is also happening as the U.S.' commitment to defense in the region becomes less clear.

"I do not think there is really any chance of a code of conduct happening with Singapore as ASEAN chair — or really, anyone as ASEAN chair," he said.

At the same time, a rushed or flawed Code would be worse than none at all, Powell said."In fact, the worst outcome is not a failure to agree, but rather a weak Code that would enable Beijing to undermine UNCLOS," he said. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which came into force in 1994, provides a comprehensive legal framework for oceans and seas globally.

"The narrative from China could then be 'see, now we have this shiny new regional agreement that overrides that problematic law invented by outsiders who don't understand East Asia and shouldn't have a say here anyway,'" Powell added.

—CNBC's Joanna Ossinger contributed to this article.

#2797. NBA Europe appears headed for 'soft launch' next fall

Commissioner Adam Silver has said he wants NBA Europe to launch in the fall of 2027 — and it appears he is going to get his wish.

Sort of. Just not in the way he or others may have originally envisioned.

There are only 11 months between now and Silver's proposed launch date, and NBA Europe has yet to have any formal agreements with teams. Negotiations with the EuroLeague — some of the teams the NBA is eyeing are members of it — have slowed. That could lead to a "soft launch" of the league next fall, reports The Athletic's Joe Vardon. A member of one of the ownership groups of a potential NBA Europe club put it this way to Vardon:

"Broadly speaking, it is implausible that a serious league could be launched (by next October)."

The idea of a "soft launch" has been floated before and is not something the NBA has pushed back on — this was always a possibility. Building something sustainable long term was always going to take time and the league understood that.

The NBA is partnering with FIBA (the international basketball organization that puts on the World Cup and helps pick teams for the Olympics) on an NBA Europe plan that calls for 12 permanent teams and four open spots teams could play their way into through domestic leagues and tournaments. Those dozen permanent teams would be made up of some existing European powerhouses — FC Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, and Panathinaikos of Greece have been mentioned, among others — plus teams in major European markets such as Rome, Paris, Lyon and others (some of those teams could be tied to existing soccer powers, but not all).

What would make things smoother is an agreement or merger with the EuroLeague — the continent's existing preeminent basketball competition — but a couple of months ago EuroLeague shareholders rejected the NBA's initial proposal. The challenge is that EuroLeague has 13 permanent members and only some of them would be jumping to NBA Europe, which is a bit messy. That said, the sides are still talking, and it's possible they reach some kind of arrangement.

What would a "soft launch" look like? From The Athletic:

So, a soft launch could, in theory, include a qualifying tournament in the fall of 2027. Another possibility for NBA Europe's 2027 version is if, as expected, the NBA formalizes agreements with at least some existing European teams to join as NBA Europe licensed franchises over the next few months. Those teams could play each other in some precursory competition that ultimately becomes NBA Europe.

NBA owners are fully backing Silver and the NBA Europe plan because it's essentially free money for them. Silver and the NBA have met with potential teams and investors and expect franchise fees in the $500 million to $1 billion range for each of the 12 permanent members.

What the NBA wants is to modernize – and better monetize — the basketball infrastructure in Europe. As part of its plan, the league is looking at a multibillion-dollar infrastructure fund to pay for arena construction, including for existing teams (which may already have arenas), bringing more modern NBA-style arenas to those cities.

He continued, "You just wanna talk s**t bout my hustle, how I'll get money, it's gonna be f**k you every time. I don't care who you are. And to me, the flip off signifies f**k professionalism."

ALSO READ: Joe Rogan Warns Ilia Topuria About Size Disadvantage at 155lbs, Urges Him to Return to Featherweight

Hokit also took aim at the growing emphasis on professionalism in MMA, arguing that it is taking away from the sport's raw and violent nature.

He added, "Professionalism is killing this sport. That's what happens when there's more money in the sport as well. People start looking at it through a professional lens and so you start fighting like that, you start point fighting. It's not about imposing your will anymore, it's about looking pretty, looking sharp. But that's not a fight at the end of the day."

The 10-1 heavyweight further explained his philosophy, saying, "We're getting locked into a cage and we're animals, we're gladiators. We can never get away from that mentality. It's about imposing your will, going forward, and who's gonna give up first."

Hokit concluded by reiterating his opposition to the growing corporate and professional image of the sport. He said, "It is what it is. And that's what happens when there's a little bit more money into it. More money, more professionalism, then you start thinking about the sport differently. And so if I have anything to do about it, I wanna try to withhold it as long as possible, as long as I'm in this game."

For the unversed, Buffer initially planned to slap Hokit's hand away if the heavyweight flipped him off during the UFC 334 main event introductions. However, he eventually decided against reacting. During a post-fight Q&A with Jon Anik, Buffer revealed exactly what had happened and how he handled the situation.

Roughly a month before the fight, Buffer had predicted to Anik and Daniel Cormier that Hokit would stick a middle finger in his face. He even revealed that his planned response was to slap the heavyweight's hand away.

Cormier, however, advised him against doing so, warning that such a reaction would risk making the moment about Buffer rather than the fighters. The veteran announcer took the advice, allowed Hokit his moment, and simply smiled back inside the Octagon.

Interestingly, the tension did not appear to linger. A few days after the event, Buffer shared a recap praising the five-round title fight against Gane, comparing it to Rocky vs. Apollo Creed. He also applauded Hokit's "warrior spirit" and even expressed interest in seeing the heavyweight compete in a rematch.

#2795. Retail investor enthusiasm for Anthropic IPO to rival SpaceX debut

Retail investor Dan Shetty is so eager to get in on the Anthropic initial public offering that he "drained" his Roth IRA and moved roughly $12,000 from Fidelity to Robinhood for a chance to participate.

"I don't want to tell my grandkids that I didn't invest in Anthropic and I didn't invest in OpenAI during the AI bubble," he said.

Shetty's enthusiasm is shared by many, with excitement among small investors for the blockbuster IPO expected to be off the charts. Vanda Research estimates that Anthropic could see approximately $250 million of retail net buying when it starts trading Thursday, double the size of SpaceX's IPO.

"That would be far and away the largest amount of net retail buying of any stock that we've seen in our data on the first day of its listing," Jai Malhi, senior strategist at Vanda, said in an interview with CNBC.

The artificial intelligence laboratory — which will trade on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol ANT — is selling 825 million shares at an expected price range of $70 to $78 per share in the IPO, though sources told CNBC the stock is likely to price above that range. Individual investors are expected to be allocated as much as 20% in that initial offering. And if Vanda's figures prove correct, the buying enthusiasm will be big as regular trading begins.

Founded less than six years ago, Anthropic aims to raise as much as $64.4 billion, giving it a valuation of $1.405 trillion. If demand is especially strong, Anthropic could even raise more than the record $85.7 billion that SpaceX sold in its record IPO in June.

The tech trade has been in turmoil since Jensen Huang's departure last week as Nvidia CEO raised questions about the future of AI financing. Before then, a potential slowdown in data center development resulting from Democratic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, and signs of moderation in the capital expenditures boom, had already spooked investors.

These all stand in marked contrast to the market backdrop in place at the time of the SpaceX IPO. In June, both positioning and sentiment were high, Malhi said. The Anthropic IPO could see a different dynamic, however. Demand could be strong across the entire investor spectrum given that sentiment is depressed, meaning that the bar to beat expectations is "much easier to overcome," he explained.

"What we're seeing across both retail and institutional positioning is that there is plenty of dry powder to take part in this IPO," the strategist said.

For the 27-year-old New Yorker Shetty, who himself works at agentic data platform Data Workers, this is his first time vying to take part in an IPO. He said Anthropic's emphasis on "safety first" drew his interest.

"I've been telling all of my friends, 'If you have like $5, you should invest it in this stock because this is the pure-play AI leader,'" Shetty said. "I think of my father who invested in Microsoft during the dotcom bubble, and he divested from that stock, and it was such a silly thing to do."

Joe Pak, a former macro portfolio manager who is now an independent researcher outside London, is opting against participating in the Anthropic IPO for two reasons: the likelihood of limited allocation and current macroeconomic conditions.

He believes the odds are probably stacked against retail investors when it comes to the allocation of shares.

"It's very difficult as a retail investor to actually get an allocation in these blockbuster IPOs," the 36-year-old said. "You get maybe one share, and the base case is you don't get any at all. So, it's a bit of a catch-22. If you do get a lot of shares, it probably means that the institutional bid was weaker, and in that case, you don't actually want the shares at that level."

In terms of the economy, conditions "need to be favorable" to hold a position in a stock like Anthropic, he said. But with the Federal Reserve having raised interest rates in September and widely expected to do so again next month, the backdrop could be darkening.

"The risk that you have is the financial conditions deteriorating" before the company starts to grow into anticipated profit and revenue, which would justify purchase of the stock, Pak said.

While Pak is steering clear of the IPO, he did say that at a certain level, it would make sense to get into Anthropic.

Other retail investors such as Bryan Nearnberg share Pak's view.

"I'm planning to eventually buy Anthropic, just not at the IPO price, considering when the lockups expire and there's some selling pressure," said the 37-year-old Westchester County, N.Y. resident, who works in finance operations. "We are not at the end of this short-term negative headline sentiment."

IPOs are a sore spot for Nearnberg, who hasn't had much luck trading stocks on their opening day. His skepticism toward IPOs can be traced all the way back to when he was in college.

"I didn't get an allocation to the Facebook IPO, but I ended up buying it the first day of open. I got burned pretty quickly," Nearnberg told CNBC. "Same thing with Zynga. I didn't get an allocation, but [got] burned pretty quickly in terms of price."

As a result of those experiences, "I'm pretty sure we'll see a good entry price underneath the IPO for Anthropic by Memorial Day next year," Nearnberg said, citing sour sentiment toward technology and concern surrounding circular financing as short-term headwinds.

To be clear, all the retail investors CNBC spoke with are optimistic on AI as a transformative technology — even the ones sitting out the IPO. One trader said he believes in AI so much that he uses Anthropic's Claude, a conversational AI assistant, every day.

"From a price-to-sales ratio, Anthropic's like a really good deal," Faigen said. But "it's still a massive valuation for a $1.4 trillion company, and there are significantly better deals out there if you are a fundamental investor."

Faigen, who works for an agentic brokerage firm, said he's "leaning towards patience," as he believes Anthropic is going to be public "for a very long time."

"I just am not in a rush to get in on day one based off the valuation," he told CNBC.

Anthropic's valuation depends on its ability to sustain its rapid growth. In the nine months through Sept. 30, revenue reached more than $33 billion, 1,200% above the year-earlier period. Aggregate spending commitments total about $900 billion, primarily centered around computing power and infrastructure.

Breakneck growth leads plenty of retail and institutional investors to approach not just the Anthropic IPO but the entire AI trade with caution.

"A lot of it comes down to scrutiny over how much money they're spending on AI," said Bret Kenwell, U.S. investment analyst at eToro. "Investors want to see that those investments are turning into tangible returns, into tangible revenue."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito contributed to this report

#2792. Big bets against AI debt, from CoreWeave to Oracle and the Mag 7, could soon hit the ETF market

Concerns about balance sheets and valuations in the artificial intelligence sector have hit the market hard since October, and investors who have shorted publicly traded tech companies in the AI trade have profited. Most investors don't think as much about "shorting" debt, but there will be a way through exchange-traded funds to profit from widening credit default swap spreads of top AI companies.

Both Tuttle Capital and Defiance ETFs have filed for funds that target the credit default swaps of companies closely linked to the AI trade, from CoreWeave and Oracle to the Magnificent Seven: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft Corporation, Nvidia, Tesla, and Apple.

Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. CDS is a closely watched indicator of issuer health in the debt markets, especially in the AI market this year. The ETFs are designed to gain when the CDS spreads of these companies widen, either as a group in the case of a Magnificent Seven CDS fund, or individually in the case of proposed ETFs targeting Oracle, CoreWeave and Meta. The funds would lose value when the market assesses the creditworthiness of these debt issuers as improving.

Both ETF managers filed for CoreWeave and Oracle CDS funds, specifically, among broader AI and semiconductor company CDS portfolios.

If the exchange-traded fund managers get approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission, these portfolios would be the first of their kind in an ETF market that has become more aggressive in recent years about launching higher-risk strategies revolving around more complex financial instruments than just public stocks and bonds. The ETF managers plan to employ leverage in the portfolios, which both increases risk and the potential for outsized returns on any given day, similar to the way existing single-stock leverage and inverse ETFs function.

The ETF managers say these CDS funds can serve an important role in a market on edge about AI debt.

"As AI infrastructure investment accelerates and companies take on significant capital commitments to fund that growth, we see an opportunity to give investors more targeted tools to manage credit risk and hedge potential financial stress across some of the biggest names driving the AI buildout," Sylvia Jablonski, CIO of Defiance ETFs, said in a statement to CNBC.

Neocloud companies like CoreWeave are a major focus for AI skeptics, an AI bubble watch compounded by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia, who is seen as a critical player in financing the AI buildout, with Nvidia called by some the "central bank of AI."

Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan on Tuesday said that neocloud company AI projects could face an existential crisis if Nvidia funding dries up. "There was a strong incentive for Nvidia as a business matter to get these projects off the ground," Rowan said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "If that banking function, that guarantor function, gets taken away, access to capital for a large number of neoclouds is going to disappear."

In its earnings filings and conference call on Tuesday, Nvidia shifted the tone in discussing the way it finances the AI ecosystem.

Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said it is less likely that these ETFs will find an audience among retail investors than smaller institutional players.

"It may be a stretch for the average retail guy," he said, but he added that having managed leveraged and inverse ETFs, it is clear that many investors "get interested" when a particular asset is seeing outsized moves, as has been the case with AI company-linked CDS in 2026. "The stuff that moves a lot is the stuff that tends to generate the most interest," he said.

Both prospectuses stress that these funds are not designed to move inversely to the reference companies' stocks and can lose money while a company's shares decline. They also note these funds don't short bonds or bet directly against a company's stock, and to buy CDS protection, they pay premiums, which are a unique cost to the fund manager whether or not credit conditions worsen.

The CDS of these companies have been on the move in a major way as part of the AI trade over the past year.

CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031 is yielding close to 16%, while spreads on its five-year credit default swaps were recently between 1,100-1,200. Spreads over 1,000 are generally considered a sign of distress.

Oracle CDS contracts have moved up over the past year from below 80 to a current range above 300.

The CDS spreads on the biggest tech companies, including Amazon and Meta as examples, rose over 100% within the past year, as their free cash flow turned negative from spending heavily on AI. Even though the market is much less concerned about their balance sheets than that of the neoclouds, major tech company CDS spreads did hit five-year highs earlier this month.

Tuttle said that these ETFs, if approved, would be the "easiest" to use for smaller institutions and family offices that want CDS exposure and "are either too small to trade with the Goldmans of the world or lack the in-house expertise to trade CDS on their own."

"It is a different way to hedge the AI trade," Tuttle said.

ETF investing experts expressed skepticism about this approach and market reception. "I don't see much demand materializing for these types of products," said Nate Geraci, president of NovaDius Wealth Management. But he added it does make sense to target these ETFs "at retail investors who are seeing scary headlines around AI capex spending. Yet another way to speculate (gamble)," he said.

Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, said he foresees confusion with how these funds will work. "How many non-professionals know what CDS are?" he said.

Tuttle says it won't take billions in assets to make an ETF focused on AI CDS a minor financial success. "My criteria is I want to see a runway to $20 million, which is about our breakeven. I see it here. It doesn't mean it will happen, but I think we have a decent chance."

—CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed to this report

Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk."

More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.

The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."

In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December.

Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability.

Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint."

"Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms."

Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off.

Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.

Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."

Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target.

The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected.

While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach.

However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028.

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act.

At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched.

Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

#2780. Chargers Week 10 PFF Grades: Del’Shawn Phillips lead spirited effort vs. Ravens rushing attack

The Chargers beat the Ravens to move to 1-8 on the season. The 0-17 jokes and hypotheticals can all finally stop.

Justin Herbert and the offense took a step forward with zero turnovers and a dominating performance on the ground with 160 yards, spurred by Omarion Hampton's 105-yard night. Herbert also added 51 yards and a rushing score, as well.

Speaking of ground games, the Chargers held the Ravens to almost nothing on the ground. All-Pro back Derrick Henry was limited to just 10 yards on 10 carries. The zero yards on the ground for Baltimore during the first half was a historic low for the franchise.

You can't be much more dominant than that.

Let's go ahead and check out the grades from Monday night.

TE Charlie Kolar – 74.8OG Logan Taylor – 74.4QB Justin Herbert – 73.0WR Tre' Harris – 72.0FB Scott Matlock – 70.2

It was poetic for Kolar — the former Baltimore Raven — to catch the first-down pass that helped seal the win over his former team. He was also dyamite in the run game, posting the second-high run block grade with a 74.6. His 76.4 pass block grade was also fourth best on the night.

Monday was Taylor's best performance as a pro, finishing with zero pressures or sacks allowed on 27 dropbacks. His 81.1 pass block grade was tops on the team while his 68.9 in run blocking was fourth best.

For the first time all season, Herbert did not throw an interception and it led to his highest game grade of 2026.

Harris caught five passes for 86 yards all in the first half. Unfortunately he caught zero passes in the final 30 minutes of game time, but his yardage still gave him a new season and career high.

During the broadcast, it was shown that, at one point, the Chargers were averaging 5.1 yards per carry with Matlock on the field and 3.8 when he was not. He's done an excellent job as the team's starting fullback and I believe the switch from a zone-heavy run scheme to a gap scheme has benefitted both him and Hampton.

OT Travis Burke – 39.5WR Quentin Johnston – 52.4OG Cole Strange – 53.4WR Derius Davis – 53.6WR Theo Wease Jr. – 54.1

Unfortunately the team's first win of the year was also one of Burke's worst performances of the season. He allowed a team-high five pressures and had an abysmal 27.9 pass block grade to go with a penalty. The next worse grade among the offensive line was Strange with an above-average 64.0.

Johnston finished with one catch on one target for six yards. His season may be one of the biggest failures for Mike McDaniel in a season packed to the brim with them.

The aforementioned Strange allowed four pressures and was also called for a penalty. His 57.3 in run block was below average but still better than Joe Alt's 53.2.

LB Del'Shawn Phillips – 90.6DT Teair Tart – 82.8CB Donte Jackson – 77.4EDGE Tuli Tuipulotu – 73.7EDGE Khalil Mack – 73.0

What a night for Phillips, and also what a season it's turning into for the first-year NFL starter. Phillips was a menace against the run on Monday night, helping the Chargers hold Derrick Henry to just 10 yards on 10 carries. He also snagged the team's only interception off Jacoby Brissett when he sprinted under a deflected by Cam Hart. All night long, his high effort was apparent.

Tart had his highest-graded game of the season overall to go with his season-high 81.7 pass rush grade. He tied a season-high of three pressures, as well.

Jackson rebounded after a rough performance against the Texans to allow just one catch for six yards in three targets his way.

Mack and Tuli combined for 15 pressures on Brissett with the latter recording a nine by himself. His previous season high was six in Week Three.

S R.J. Mickens – 25.1CB Deane Leonard – 28.5S Elijah Molden – 40.9LB Daiyan Henley – 51.7DT Jamaree Caldwell – 53.9

Mickens luckily knocked down the Hail Mary attempt by the Ravens to seal the team's first win of the season, but it was otherwise a bad night for the second-year safety. His overall game grade was his worst of the year by far and his 26.6 coverage grade was very much the same. Mickens was also called for his third penalty of the season.

Molden was credited with allowing five receptions on six targets towards him for 65 yards, including 53 after the catch. Henley also was dinged a bunch in coverage. PFF has him credited with a whopping nine receptions allowed on 11 targets in his area.

#2778. CEO turned informant: How the FDA built a case against executives promising cheap medications

The federal case against an alleged illegal prescription drug operation and its two top leaders earlier this month features a notable informant: the CEO of a peer company that authorities say was committing the same import violations.

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and director of a Canadian healthcare company called CANARX, was arrested in the tunnel connecting Detroit and Canada on Nov. 8 and charged with smuggling, conspiracy and importing a misbranded drug for patient use in the United States. His brother and the president of the company, Bob Howard, is wanted on similar charges and was still being sought as of last week, according to court records.

The charges mark the first criminal case by U.S. authorities against a company that's part of a cottage industry known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, that promise to lower or eliminate high prescription drug costs for Americans.

The cheaper medications are typically sourced from international markets, a business model that the Food and Drug Administration and Department of Homeland Security say is illegal and can put patients' health at risk.

At issue is the unregulated nature of drugs intended for foreign markets and, in some cases, the risk of counterfeit products. And while AFPs generally argue that the importation of medication is allowable under U.S. law by individuals for personal use, authorities contend the operations go too far.

CANARX, based in Windsor, Ontario, was established in 2002 and was featured in a CNBC investigation into the booming AFP industry.

Joseph Morris, general counsel for CANARX, told CNBC last year that the business was operating legally and was confident in the safety of the prescriptions it provided. Last week, Morris told CNBC that the Howard brothers "deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court."

The FDA's case against CANARX started with a tip about a similar healthcare operation called ScriptSourcing. It is detailed in a 35-page affidavit — dated Oct. 29 and unsealed last week — written by Dustin Dobbs, special agent with the FDA's Office of Criminal Investigations.

Based in Bonita Springs, Florida, ScriptSourcing marketed its international prescription program to self-funded employer health plans. Founder and CEO Gary Becker was described on the company's website as a "health insurance and risk management consultant for more than 30 years."

ScriptSourcing had been on the FDA's radar since at least 2022 for potential drug import violations, according to the affidavit. In August 2025, Dobbs, posing as someone interested in the AFP business, emailed ScriptSourcing and asked if the company was FDA-compliant.

A ScriptSourcing employee in responses to Dobbs said the company was FDA-compliant and that it had more than 2,000 name brand specialty medications and worked with more than 3,000 self-funded health plans.

However, that same year, the agency learned of two alleged incidents in which medications from ScriptSourcing's international drug import program had harmed patients, according to Dobbs' affidavit. One patient had been hospitalized due to a small bowel obstruction after she used misbranded Mounjaro sourced by the company via a Canadian pharmacy, and another was allegedly seriously injured after receiving a counterfeit medication.

Facing scrutiny from the FDA, ScriptSourcing CEO Becker turned on the Howard brothers of CANARX.

By May 2026, Becker had become a cooperating witness for the government in its investigation into the Canadian firm, Dobbs wrote. Becker told the FDA that he had done business with CANARX on drug importation and that the company had given him a "road map" on how to operate, according to the affidavit.

ScriptSourcing provided the FDA with a spreadsheet of financial transactions with CANARX between 2021 and 2026. It showed approximately 16,549 prescription drugs have been dispensed, the affidavit said.

Then, in several recorded phone calls between June and July 2026, Becker discussed the foreign importations with the Howard brothers.

The phone calls "show that John Howard was aware of the routes for importation of drugs from Canada into the United States and has tried to mold them to fit [CANARX's] illegal drug importation program," Dobbs wrote in the affidavit. "These phone calls also show that John Howard and Bob Howard were aware that these drugs were not allowed to enter into the United States legally."

Among the shipments en route or being prepared by CANARX at the time the information was provided was a package that contained Neupro, an FDA-regulated drug for the treatment of Parkinson's disease and restless legs syndrome.

The FDA did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC on the details in the affidavit.

Gary Becker's attorney, George Karavetsos, declined to comment when reached by CNBC, but confirmed on Monday that ScriptSourcing was no longer in business.

The AFP business model was at the center of a civil lawsuit originally filed by Gilead Sciences in December 2024 that alleged several companies, including CANARX, illegally imported its HIV drug Biktarvy. CANARX has not responded to Gilead's allegations.

Gilead said in a statement to CNBC last week in response to charges against the Howard brothers that it "welcomed the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk."

"Pharmaceuticals manufactured for foreign markets are almost always considered unapproved and misbranded drugs under U.S. law, whether counterfeit or even if made by the same manufacturer that produced the version sold in the United States," Dobbs wrote in his affidavit.

— CNBC's Melissa Lee and Paige Tortorelli contributed to this report.

The Miami Heat played host to the Milwaukee Bucks on Wednesday night. While this was already a big game — the first time Giannis Antetokounmpo is facing his former team — it carried even more meaning.

The long-awaited "GTA VI" releases nationwide on Thursday. It is arguably the most highly anticipated video game of all time, coming out 13 years after GTA V was released back in 2013.

The game, which has already received near-perfect reviews, is set to upend the world Thursda. With estimates that roughly 16 million copies of the game were pre-ordered, employers could be dealing with a lot of "sick" days ahead of the weekend.

That might sound far-fetched, but it's true. Experts are estimating businesses in the United States could lose over $1 billion in productivity due to worker absences.

"Vice City" is a fictional city from the franchise. It is not a direct replica of Miami, but it is heavily inspired by the city, while the state of "Leonida" in the video game is inspired by Florida.

The Heat's marketing department took the chance to host a "Vice City"-inspired night in honor of the game's release, and it just so happened to coincide with Anteokounmpo getting his first crack at his old team.

ESPN reporter Cam Wolf showed that fans lined up four hours before tipoff in the rain to get access to the "Vice City"-inspired gear that was selling in the team store.

#2776. Get them out! Gary Neville tells Mauricio Pochettino to axe SIX Manchester United stars including Marcus Rashford

Gary Neville has called for a brutal summer clear-out at Manchester United, urging incoming manager Mauricio Pochettino to offload six high-profile stars. The legendary full-back believes the current squad requires a total overhaul to escape their current slump near the foot of the Premier League table.

Pochettino has taken over from Michael Carrick at Carrington just three days before Manchester United travel to face Liverpool on November 22. The incoming boss inherits a side sitting 18th in the Premier League with only one win from 10 matches, having already exited the Carabao Cup following a September home defeat to Brighton.

Supporters have vented their frustration by booing the players at Old Trafford, though Gary Neville has defended Diogo Dalot as an unfair scapegoat due to his work-rate. Instead, Neville expects Pochettino to move on Noussair Mazraoui, Matthijs de Ligt, Mason Mount, Marcus Rashford, and Joshua Zirkzee at the end of the campaign, while Lisandro Martinez is anticipated to depart when his contract expires next summer.

Speaking on Stick to United, Neville sprang to Dalot's defence after the Portuguese full-back was jeered by home supporters.

"Do I think Dalot is Denis Irwin? No. Denis Irwin is the greatest full-back Manchester United have ever had, I shouldn't be mentioning him in the same breath, but I would get rid of a few before Dalot," Neville said. "Dalot's been shoved onto that left-hand side. [Ruben] Amorim had him at left-wing back dying, it was awful to watch. So he's literally sticking his hand up and saying, 'I'll play there. I'll do anything for the team.' I never see him shirk anything.

"He's not an amazing player, let's be clear. He never shirks anything. I think if he was in a decent back four, he'd be all right. But he's got a shocking back four alongside him. Positionally he's not great, he could be better on the ball. I just think he's such an easy target."

Rather than offloading Dalot, Neville argued that United's unavailable defensive options must be cleared out first. "I'd be getting rid of Mazraoui well before him. Martinez, De Ligt... De Ligt doesn't play football. If a player is injury-prone and doesn't play football, just because he hasn't played it doesn't mean he should go above a player who's played every single week and is throwing his hand up. You want someone who's actually reliable and available to play. So De Ligt has to go."

Assessing the squad, Neville outlined which players Pochettino will look to retain. Neville said: "New goalkeeper... I think he'll want someone to compete with [Senne] Lammens, I'm not saying he changes Lammens, I think we saw enough last season to carry on with him. Defenders... he'll keep [Luke] Shaw because he knows him and he'll probably get the best out of him. The problem with Luke is injuries and you'll have to manage him. He'll keep [Harry] Maguire because he'll trust him and think he's a soldier, someone who can do a job for him. He'll keep [Leny] Yoro because he'll think there's something to work with. [Ayden] Heaven, I'd loan him out, get some experience in the Championship. He's nowhere near it, it's unfair to put him in the situation he's in."

In midfield, Neville backed Pochettino to work with several younger and established options while cutting Mount loose. "I'd keep Bruno [Fernandes], Kobbie [Mainoo], [Youri] Tielemans. Mount would have to go, [Andrey] Santos… Mauricio may like him because he's young, mobile, and aggressive, he might get something out of him. Him and [Carlos] Baleba will be in that middle bit. Mount's the one that goes in that midfield section."

Up front, wage constraints and tactical fit will dictate who survives the overhaul. "Zirkzee definitely to go. I think Marcus 100 per cent to go because he's on massive money and that story has been well told. They can't afford to pay him that money, you have to get rid of that wage at the earliest opportunity. He'll work with Amad [Diallo], he'll work with [Bryan] Mbeumo, he'll work with [Matheus] Cunha, and he'll work with [Benjamin] Sesko. He'll use [Patrick] Dorgu in the short term but he'll be one who will go in the next couple of years. [Manuel] Ugarte will go, 100 per cent."

Pochettino faces an immediate test away to Liverpool on Sunday as he attempts to halt United's slide down the Premier League table, yet Neville believes fixing the squad will require a phased clear-out across consecutive summers. "If you look through it now I'd say Martinez would go, De Ligt would go, Mazraoui would go, Mount would go, first wave next summer. Rashford if you can, and Zirkzee. And then the year after you'd be looking at Shaw, Maguire, Dalot, Bruno, that's your second wave and maybe then you've made your mind up on Baleba and Santos."

With senior figures like Fernandes, Maguire and Shaw earmarked for the second phase of departures, quick fixes remain unrealistic at Old Trafford. "But the earliest Mauricio Pochettino can unravel this squad is two seasons if he does well. It could take three to get this squad unravelled," Neville concluded.

#2775. Kash Patel skips House hearing after Mar-a-Lago gala with $50,000 access

After a string of outages disrupted airlines, banks and even the National Security Agency, U.S. House members gathered Wednesday to question the nation's top security officials. But FBI Director Kash Patel was nowhere to be seen.

The night before, Patel and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had been advertised as "honored guests" at the Big Blue Bash, a lavish charitable fundraiser at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, where attendees were offered access to a "private roundtable" and a stay at the venue for $50,000 a person.

Mullin appeared before lawmakers Wednesday morning at the committee's annual threat assessment hearing. Patel sent his deputy instead. And as the hearing got underway, a Justice Department jet that's been used by Patel before was still flying back from Florida.Flight records reviewed by CNBC show the Justice Department aircraft associated with Patel's travel left West Palm Beach, Florida, at 7:51 a.m. Wednesday and landed at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington at 10:20 a.m. — 20 minutes after the House Homeland Security Committee hearing began.

The FBI confirmed Patel, Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche attended the Mar-a-Lago event.

"The event is approved by Ethics, following all guidelines and regulations," FBI spokesperson Benjamin Williamson told CNBC by email, noting the gala "is an annual event honoring fallen law enforcement officers and their families."

Patel's absence drew bipartisan criticism on Capitol Hill. Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., said lawmakers had spent months trying to secure Patel's testimony, only for the FBI director to make clear he had "no intention" of appearing.

Rep. Bennie Thompson, of Mississippi, the committee's top Democrat, said Patel's absence for a second consecutive year undermined lawmakers' ability to conduct oversight. Prior to 2024, FBI directors traditionally testified at the annual hearing.

The episode also drew attention to what was being offered at Trump's private club: a chance for donors and corporate sponsors to meet privately with some of the nation's most powerful law enforcement officials.

"Trump's Big Blue Bash is yet another fundraising event that encourages wealthy special interests, particularly those seeking lucrative government contracts, to rub elbows with officials responsible for awarding those contracts," Craig Holman, a government ethics and lobbying expert at the watchdog group Public Citizen, told CNBC.

Billed as a tribute to federal officers and their families, the second annual black-tie gala came with a price list for access.

General admission cost nearly $5,000, a VIP all-access pass $25,000 and a private roundtable with federal agency heads and a night at Trump's resort $50,000, according to the event's ticketing page. A sponsorship prospectus reviewed by CNBC advertised corporate packages reaching $1 million, including private briefings, speaking time and the chance to name and present an award to a federal agency of the sponsor's choosing.

Alongside Patel and Mullin, the advertised guest list also included White House border czar Tom Homan and leaders of Customs and Border Protection, the Secret Service, Drug Enforcement Administration and Transportation Security Administration.

It remains unclear which officials attended private meetings or which companies bought the most expensive packages. But several sponsors had substantial business with the agencies represented.

Motorola Solutions, the gala's top named sponsor, had approximately $237.1 million in fiscal 2026 net contract obligations from the Justice and Homeland Security departments, according to CNBC's analysis of federal records. That included a $139.6 million Bureau of Prisons radio contract, a $25.8 million Customs and Border Protection award and a nearly $18 million Secret Service contract option, all in September.

Motorola reported roughly $1.69 million in federal lobbying expenses this year through September, according to its first-quarter, second-quarter and third-quarter disclosures. Its lobbying included homeland security funding, communications technology and other issues.

"Motorola Solutions was proud to support last night's Big Blue Bash, honoring the families of wounded and fallen federal officers, whom we hosted as the night's guests of honor," the company said through a spokesperson. "We did not participate in private briefings."

Two other federal contractors, the Vierra Group and Teya Diversified Services, sponsored a Department of Homeland Security presentation featuring Mullin and Homan, according to the gala's published program.

Federal contracting records show Teya received three Customs and Border Protection contracts in September worth approximately $23.3 million combined for repairs at northern border ports of entry. The awards included $9.1 million for work at 12 ports, $7.9 million for nine ports and $6.4 million for 10 ports.

LEO Technologies, which markets artificial intelligence and surveillance products to law enforcement agencies, was also listed as a sponsor.

Vierra, Teya and LEO Technologies didn't immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

Federal ethics rules require authorization for officials to participate in charitable fundraising in their official capacities and restrict the use of government titles for personal fundraising.

Holman said companies attending such events hope to gain favor with the administration and ultimately benefit through government contracts and policies affecting their businesses.

There is no evidence the sponsorships influenced federal contracts or secured preferential treatment, and some new contract awards added to existing contracts.

The financial questions extend to Trump's own business. Organizers haven't disclosed what Mar-a-Lago was paid or how much reached the Federal Law Enforcement Officers Foundation, the nonprofit that's the event's beneficiary. The gala offered a $1 million sponsorship package — more than the charity's entire 2024 revenue of $725,476, according to its latest available IRS filing — though no purchase has been confirmed. A Republican fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago cost about $318,000 in 2023, according to a New York Times analysis of campaign finance records.

The event also may raise questions about taxpayer-funded travel. Organizers listed Mullin as a speaker, and flight records reviewed by CNBC show a Gulfstream jet registered to DHS arriving in West Palm Beach Tuesday evening, alongside the Justice Department plane associated with Patel's travel. It remains unclear who was aboard either aircraft or whether the flights were connected to the gala.

Days earlier, Mullin used a government plane to attend a Louisiana State University football game shortly after a nationwide FAA ground stop. He defended the trip Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee, saying government travel was required and that he personally paid for it.

#2774. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."
